name: Otsu and adaptive MNDWI thresholding, plus sub-pixel water fraction

identity.method_name: Otsu (1979) automatic histogram thresholding and Donchyts-style adaptive/edge-based thresholding applied to MNDWI (Xu 2006), plus sub-pixel water-fraction estimation via linear spectral mixture analysis (LSMA) / fully constrained least squares (FCLS)
identity.core_idea: Instead of the project's fixed rule MNDWI>0, Otsu's method picks, per histogram, the threshold that maximises between-class variance (equivalently minimises within-class variance) assuming the pixel population is bimodal (water vs. not-water); it can be run globally per scene, locally per lake window, or restricted to a buffer around detected water/land edges (the 'edge-Otsu' variant of Donchyts et al. 2016). Sub-pixel water fraction instead treats each 20 m pixel's reflectance as a linear mixture of a small number of pure endmember spectra (water, vegetation, bare soil/built-up) and solves a non-negativity- and sum-to-one-constrained least squares problem (FCLS) per pixel, returning a continuous 0-100% water estimate rather than a binary in/out label. All three variants remove the single fixed cutoff, but none of them add any new information the sensor did not already record -- they only change how the same MNDWI/reflectance values are converted into a water/not-water (or percent-water) call.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. These are algorithms, not datasets, applied to the project's own cached Sentinel-2 L2A bands (Earth Search STAC, tile MGRS-43PGQ, B02/B03/B04/B08/B11 on the 20 m EPSG:32643 grid). The JRC Global Surface Water product (Pekel et al. 2016, doi 10.1038/nature20584) and ESA WorldCover are mentioned below only as possible external cross-checks, not as inputs.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Fully unsupervised for Otsu and adaptive thresholding -- both are pure histogram/statistics operations on the scene's own pixel values and need no labels of any kind, at zero labelling cost. Sub-pixel LSMA/FCLS is also fully unsupervised in the sense that it needs no encroachment labels, but it is not entirely label-free in practice: it requires the analyst to designate 2-3 endmember spectra (pure water, pure vegetation/hyacinth, pure bare soil/built-up), typically by hand-picking a handful of unambiguous pixels per class from the scene itself or from a spectral library. That endmember-picking step costs roughly 0.5-1 student-day per representative scene and is itself an unsupervised design choice, not a supervised label, but it is a real degree of freedom that must be documented because a poorly chosen endmember set silently biases every fraction estimate downstream.
fit_to_project.input_required: The same five cached Sentinel-2 bands already used to compute MNDWI (B03 green, B11 SWIR at minimum; B02/B04/B08 useful as extra unmixing bands). Nothing new needs to be acquired for Otsu or adaptive thresholding. Sub-pixel LSMA additionally needs a chosen endmember spectral set, which can be extracted from the project's own imagery (no external acquisition required) but does need deliberate curation.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes-if-reframed. None of these three variants is a per-lake-year model; each is a per-scene, per-pixel computation. The effective sample size for Otsu is one histogram per scene (42 scenes: 6 lakes x 7 years, or fewer if global-per-scene thresholds are shared across lakes captured in the same tile date), and for sub-pixel fraction it is one value per pixel per scene (a few hundred to a few thousand lake-interior pixels x 42 scene-dates). The 42-row ceiling that constrains the tabular model does not constrain these methods directly; they simply produce an alternative version of the single 'water area' number that already feeds each of the 42 rows.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes for Otsu and edge-Otsu adaptive thresholding (fully automatic, no ground truth needed by construction). needs-weak-labels in a narrow sense for sub-pixel LSMA/FCLS, because endmember selection is a human-in-the-loop design step (see ground_truth_proxy_strategy); it is not encroachment ground truth, only a spectral-purity choice, but it should not be described as fully automatic.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Otsu and adaptive thresholding operate natively on the project's existing 20 m grid with no assumption mismatch. Sub-pixel fraction mapping is specifically motivated by exactly this project's resolution problem: the project already downsamples the native 10 m optical bands (B02/B03/B04/B08) to a common 20 m grid to match the 20 m SWIR band (B11), which discards resolution that would otherwise help resolve small, narrow, or partially-flooded shorelines. The cited method in doi 10.3390/w15081446 (DE_MRF, Water 2023) does exactly this: it starts from 10 m/20 m Sentinel-2 bands and produces a finer sub-pixel water-fraction map (2 m target resolution in that paper's Jinshui Basin case study), which is directly relevant to recovering some of the resolution the project's own 20 m regridding step throws away, and is most valuable precisely for the smallest lake in the dataset (Sankey Tank, ~310 pixels at 20 m = 12.4 ha).
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: none for Otsu/adaptive thresholding; a small hand-picked endmember set (drawn from the project's own imagery, not an external label) for sub-pixel LSMA/FCLS.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four stated limitations directly. It does not add rows (1), does not touch OpenStreetMap building data (2), does not create ground truth (3) -- it remains just as unsupervised and just as unvalidated as the current fixed threshold -- and does not add more scenes per year (4). Its only indirect benefit is to the quality of the single 'water area' input feature that already exists inside the 42-row table, and, for sub-pixel fraction specifically, a partial mitigation of the 20 m regridding's own information loss.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. A drained lakebed during desilting is spectrally bare soil/mud, and every one of these methods will correctly report it as near-zero water (Otsu, adaptive, and LSMA alike) -- exactly like the current fixed MNDWI>0 threshold already does. None of them has any mechanism to distinguish 'temporarily drained for engineered desilting' from 'permanently filled in for encroachment'; that distinction requires evidence outside the water-index/water-fraction number entirely (temporal shape analysis as in C9, or independent documentary evidence such as desilting tenders or news reports).
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, and this is a genuine limitation shared by all three variants. Water hyacinth mats are spectrally vegetation (high NDVI/NIR, low MNDWI), so Otsu and adaptive thresholding will classify hyacinth-covered water as 'not water', reproducing the existing confound exactly. A 2-endmember (water/land) LSMA does the same thing in continuous form: hyacinth-covered pixels get a ~0% water fraction, not because the method is more accurate, but because optical sensors genuinely cannot see through a floating mat. A 3-endmember unmixing (water, hyacinth/vegetation, bare soil) built against the published Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843) as an independent cross-check could in principle report a separate hyacinth fraction, but this is an extension beyond what a standard water-fraction LSMA does and is not demonstrated in the cited sub-pixel papers.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None beyond what the current method already has. All three variants are still applied inside, and aggregated to, the OpenStreetMap lake multipolygon, which per project_constraints.lake_boundary is not a legal or cadastral boundary. Switching the water-detection RULE does not change what polygon the resulting area is measured against; whichever buffer distance (30 m reinstated Master Plan buffer, or the quashed 75 m NGT buffer) is tested downstream is unaffected by this item.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Every scene's Otsu/adaptive threshold and every pixel's fraction estimate is recomputed fresh per year (unlike the OSM building counts), so the underlying reflectance input genuinely varies year to year. But the project still captures only one dry-season scene per year (project_constraints.imagery), so none of these methods add temporal density; they only change how each already-existing annual snapshot is converted into a number. A year-to-year 'threshold' that itself moves (because Otsu is recomputed per scene) also introduces a new, harder-to-audit source of apparent year-to-year variance that a single fixed threshold does not have.

implementation.libraries: skimage.filters.threshold_otsu (scikit-image) for classic global Otsu; numpy/scipy for a from-scratch local/windowed or edge-based (Canny + buffer + Otsu, following Donchyts et al. 2016) implementation; scipy.optimize.nnls or pysptools (unmixing module: NNLS/FCLS) for fully constrained least squares sub-pixel unmixing; rasterio/rioxarray for band I/O on the existing 20 m grid.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable. All three variants are classical, parameter-free-or-few-parameter statistical/algebraic procedures computed fresh on each scene; there are no weights to load or fine-tune.
implementation.licence: Fully open. scikit-image (BSD-3), scipy (BSD-3), pysptools (GPL-3 -- check compatibility if the rest of the project's code is more permissively licensed) are all usable in an academic project; Sentinel-2 L2A data is open under the Copernicus data licence. No licence blocker.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial for all three. Global or per-lake Otsu on a 20 m grid runs in well under a second per scene; edge-Otsu (Canny + buffered histogram sampling) is only marginally more expensive; FCLS unmixing on a few thousand lake-interior pixels solves in milliseconds per scene. No GPU is needed anywhere in this item; it is fully reproducible on a laptop CPU by a solo student.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 1-2 student-days for global and per-lake-windowed Otsu plus an edge-Otsu variant, run and compared against the fixed threshold across all 42 lake-years; an additional 2-3 student-days for sub-pixel LSMA/FCLS, most of which is spent on endmember selection, sanity-checking unmixing residuals, and deciding how to aggregate a continuous fraction map back into a single 'water area' number comparable to the current pixel-counting method. Total for the full comparison (a)+(b)+(c): about 3-5 student-days.

evaluation.metrics: Absolute and percentage difference in estimated water area (hectares) between the fixed threshold, Otsu, adaptive/edge-Otsu, and the aggregated sub-pixel fraction, reported per lake-year; for LSMA/FCLS, the per-pixel unmixing residual (root-sum-of-squares of unexplained reflectance after fitting the endmember mixture) as a self-diagnostic of fit quality -- this is a genuine, ground-truth-free quality signal, since a high residual flags pixels or scenes where the linear two/three-endmember model does not describe the observed spectrum well (e.g. turbid or hyacinth-covered water). Accuracy metrics (precision/recall/kappa against a true water mask) cannot be computed at all, because no ground-truth water mask exists for any of the 42 lake-years.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a trained model, so no train/test split applies in the conventional sense. The appropriate protocol is a temporal and cross-method sensitivity analysis: run all threshold variants across all 42 lake-years and report where they diverge, plus a small manual visual-inspection subset (true-colour and false-colour Sentinel-2 composites for the years that matter most -- Sankey Tank across all years, and Bellandur/Varthur 2019-2021-2025) as an informal sanity check, explicitly labelled as non-statistical spot-checking rather than validation.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Minimal in the classical train/test sense since nothing is fit and reused, but there is a real circularity risk if sub-pixel endmembers are hand-picked from the SAME lake-year scene being unmixed and then that scene's fraction estimate is reported as an independent improvement -- the endmember choice can be tuned, consciously or not, to produce a result that looks more plausible. The mitigation is to fix a single global endmember set (or one per broad scene-date/atmospheric condition) chosen independently of any specific lake-year's outcome, and to disclose that choice.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None of the three variants produces a calibrated uncertainty interval by default. Otsu and adaptive thresholding output a single bare threshold and a single bare area number per scene; a bootstrap over sub-samples of the scene's own pixels could yield an empirical threshold confidence interval at modest extra cost, but this is not standard practice and is not implemented in the cited work. FCLS unmixing's residual (above) is a useful per-pixel diagnostic but is not a calibrated confidence interval on the fraction estimate itself. Given the project has no ground truth anywhere, reporting a bare point estimate from any of these methods without at least the bootstrap-threshold or unmixing-residual diagnostic is hard to defend.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable. No synthetic data generation, resampling for class balance, or time-series interpolation is involved in any of the three variants; they operate directly on real, unaugmented per-pixel reflectance.

evidence.published_performance: Otsu's original method (Otsu 1979, IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 9(1):62-66) is foundational and reports no water-specific accuracy figure -- it is a generic bimodal-histogram algorithm. Donchyts et al. 2016 (Remote Sensing 8(5):386, doi 10.3390/rs8050386) report that naive whole-scene Otsu/global thresholding becomes unreliable specifically when water occupies a small fraction of the scene, motivating their edge-buffered ('edge-Otsu') sampling approach used operationally in the JRC/Google Earth Engine surface-water pipeline; exact quantitative accuracy figures from that paper were not independently re-derived here [verify]. The Water 2022 SAR study (doi 10.3390/w14244030) documents the same minority-class failure for backscatter-based thresholding of small flooded areas [verify exact figures before quoting]. doi 10.3390/w15081446 (DE_MRF, Water 2023) reports that their sub-pixel morphological-dilation-erosion plus Markov random field method improves surface-water delineation accuracy over hard-classified Sentinel-2 masks in heterogeneous, small-water-body terrain in the Jinshui Basin, China, with reported overall accuracy gains over hard thresholding [verify exact percentage-point figures against the primary paper]. doi 10.1080/15481603.2023.2217573 (GIScience & Remote Sensing 2023) reports that regression-based sub-pixel fraction mapping using a synthetic spectral library improves small-water-body (pond/reservoir-scale) area estimation accuracy relative to hard classification, again with specific numeric gains that require direct confirmation against the paper [verify].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Donchyts et al. 2016: Murray-Darling Basin, Australia (large semi-arid basin, not small urban lakes). doi 10.3390/w15081446: Jinshui Basin, China -- a rural/agricultural river basin with heterogeneous small water bodies, not an urban lake system. doi 10.1080/15481603.2023.2217573: small water bodies (ponds, on-farm reservoirs) in an unspecified/synthetic-library-driven study setting distinct from Bengaluru's urban tank system [uncertain -- exact study site not independently confirmed]. None of the cited primary sources study urban lakes carrying a hyacinth or desilting confound of the kind documented for Bellandur/Varthur.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No direct application of Otsu, edge-Otsu adaptive thresholding, or sub-pixel LSMA/FCLS to Bengaluru or Indian urban lakes specifically was found in this search. The most relevant Bengaluru-specific evidence remains the Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte-cover mapping (MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843), which is a mapping study, not a thresholding-method study, and should be used only as an independent cross-check dataset, not as evidence that these specific thresholding methods have been validated locally.
evidence.evidence_recency: 1979 (Otsu, foundational, explicitly in-range per the brief's own carve-out) and 2006 (Xu, MNDWI, likewise in-range); 2016 (Donchyts adaptive/edge-Otsu); 2022-2023 for the small-water-body and sub-pixel fraction evidence (both cited DOIs are 2023). No item in this file relies solely on pre-2020 evidence for its central, non-foundational claim.
evidence.primary_sources: Otsu, N. (1979), 'A threshold selection method from gray-level histograms', IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 9(1):62-66. Xu, H. (2006), 'Modification of normalised difference water index (NDWI) to enhance open water features in remotely sensed imagery', International Journal of Remote Sensing 27(14):3025-3033, https://doi.org/10.1080/01431160600589179 . Donchyts, G. et al. (2016), 'A 30 m Resolution Surface Water Mask Including Estimation of Positional and Thematic Differences Using Landsat 8, SRTM and OpenStreetMap: A Case Study in the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia', Remote Sensing 8(5):386, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs8050386 . Pekel, J.-F. et al. (2016), 'High-resolution mapping of global surface water and its long-term changes', Nature 540:418-422, https://doi.org/10.1038/nature20584 (JRC Global Surface Water, cited only as a possible external cross-check dataset). 'A Self-Adaptive Thresholding Approach for Automatic Water Extraction Using Sentinel-1 SAR Imagery Based on OTSU Algorithm and Distance Block', Remote Sensing 15(10):2690 (2023), https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15102690 [additional adaptive-Otsu context, not independently deep-read here -- verify before quoting]. Sub-pixel water mapping: https://doi.org/10.3390/w15081446 (Water, 2023). Sub-pixel water fraction regression: https://doi.org/10.1080/15481603.2023.2217573 (GIScience & Remote Sensing, 2023). Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte cross-check: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12223843 (Remote Sensing, 2020).

risk.failure_modes: (1) Class-imbalance collapse: Otsu's between-class-variance maximisation assumes a roughly bimodal histogram; when water is a tiny minority of the pixel population (Sankey Tank's ~310 pixels are roughly 0.03% of the ~900,000-pixel scene, and Bellandur 2021 had almost no water at all), the histogram is effectively unimodal, the between-class-variance function has no clear, stable maximum, and Otsu can return a degenerate threshold that classifies almost all or almost none of the scene as water -- this is a textbook, well-documented failure mode, not a hypothetical one. (2) Windowing does not rescue the worst cases: restricting Otsu to a local window around each lake polygon increases the water fraction of the sampled histogram for lakes that HAVE substantial water, but for a lake in a near-total-drainage state (Bellandur 2021) the local window is itself dominated by bare, wet, or turbid lakebed, not a clean bimodal water/land split, so local windowing does not fix the exact years the project cares about most. (3) Edge-Otsu needs a detectable edge: the Donchyts-style buffered-edge sampling approach requires an actual water/land boundary to exist in the scene; in a near-zero-water year it may find no reliable edge, and its behaviour degrades to the same failure as global Otsu. (4) LSMA/FCLS endmember sensitivity: turbid urban lake water, algal blooms, and partially hyacinth-covered water all violate the assumption that a small, fixed set of pure endmembers can describe every pixel, biasing fraction estimates in ways that are hard to detect without ground truth. (5) Threshold instability adds noise: because Otsu recomputes a new threshold per scene, atmospheric or seasonal reflectance shifts can move the threshold year to year in a way a fixed rule does not, converting the current method's stable, well-understood bias into a less predictable, harder-to-audit source of year-to-year variance.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask precisely the question the task poses: would switching to Otsu change the headline numbers, and can you tell? The only defensible answer is the direct one: for lakes and years with substantial persistent water, Otsu is expected to move the area estimate only modestly (a few percent) relative to the fixed MNDWI>0 threshold, but for exactly the two hardest, most analytically important cases in the dataset -- Sankey Tank (310 pixels, permanently near the minority-class threshold) and Bellandur 2021 (near-zero water) -- Otsu is expected to become numerically unstable, which should be reported as a demonstrated limitation of Otsu, not as a competing headline number. On validation without ground truth, the honest answer is that no formal accuracy validation is possible; the best available checks are (a) visual inspection of true/false-colour composites for a handful of critical lake-years, (b) cross-referencing the Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte paper as an independent, though narrow, external anchor, and (c) reporting cross-method agreement/divergence across the 42 lake-years as a sensitivity analysis, explicitly not as an accuracy score.
risk.honest_expectation: For lakes with a clearly bimodal water/land histogram and a normal, non-drought year, Otsu will likely produce an area estimate close to (within roughly a few percent of) the current fixed-threshold estimate -- not a large or dramatic change to the project's overall narrative. For Sankey Tank in every year, and for Bellandur specifically in 2021, Otsu is expected to be unreliable or unstable, and this instability is itself the most useful, reportable finding from this item: it is direct evidence for why the project should retain the fixed MNDWI>0 threshold as its primary, documented method, and use Otsu only as a disclosed robustness/sensitivity check, not a replacement. Sub-pixel water-fraction estimation is the more promising piece of this item for the small-lake problem specifically, since a continuous percent-water number is less brittle than a hard in/out call for a 310-pixel lake, but it resolves neither the desilting nor the hyacinth confound and costs several extra student-days to implement credibly.

verdict.recommended_rank: consider-with-reasons for Otsu/adaptive thresholding, run only as a disclosed sensitivity/robustness check against the fixed threshold, never as a silent replacement, because its own well-documented minority-class failure mode is directly triggered by this project's smallest lake and driest year. adopt-if-time for sub-pixel water-fraction estimation as a supplementary continuous metric, given the extra 2-3 student-days it costs and that it fixes neither confound.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We tested Otsu thresholding as a sensitivity check against our fixed MNDWI>0 threshold and found it becomes numerically unstable exactly where it matters most -- Sankey Tank's tiny 310-pixel footprint and Bellandur's near-zero 2021 water -- so we kept the fixed threshold as the documented primary method and, time permitting, added a sub-pixel water-fraction estimate as a continuous supplementary measure rather than a hard replacement, none of which can be validated against ground truth we do not have.
